children: face fresh uncertainty over one of the U.K.'s most important North Sea gas projects after Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government reportedly delayed a decision on the Jackdaw field until after an Oct. 8 parliamentary by-election. For investors, the delay pushes a key regulatory catalyst deeper into the year and reinforces the political risk surrounding large U.K. oil and gas developments even as Britain faces concerns about winter energy supply.

Jackdaw is part of Adura, the North Sea joint venture owned 50-50 by Shell and Equinor. Adura combines the companies' U.K. offshore portfolios and is expected to produce more than 140,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day in 2026, making it the country's largest independent North Sea producer.

The Jackdaw decision had reportedly been expected as soon as this week but is now likely to slip into late autumn. The timing allows the government to avoid a politically sensitive ruling before both the Holborn and St Pancras by-election and Labour's party conference, where new North Sea development faces resistance from parts of the party.

The delay matters because Jackdaw is not a marginal project. Shell has previously estimated that peak production could equal more than 6% of projected U.K. North Sea gas output, enough energy to heat roughly 1.4 million homes.

Significant infrastructure is already in place. Shell said earlier this year that Jackdaw was expected to become operational in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to regulatory approval, after offshore installation work progressed during 2025.
The immediate catalyst is now the government's post-election decision and whether approval arrives early enough to avoid additional schedule slippage.
Investors should watch for any change to Jackdaw's expected start-up timetable, further environmental or legal challenges and whether Rosebank faces similar political delays.

For Shell and Equinor, one delayed project is manageable. A broader pattern of slower North Sea approvals, however, could raise development costs, reduce production visibility and make future U.K. investment less attractive.

title: Shell's Troubled Project Faces Another Major Blow
